title: SLA token-cost vs quality sweep — INT8 / AWQ / FP8 (sparse kernels)
content:
Summary:

We ran a targeted sweep oriented around customer SLAs to understand cost (per-token), latency tail behavior, and degradations in output quality across three quant families: INT8 (symmetric/affine), AWQ (blockwise asymmetric), and FP8 (e4m3-like low-precision) with both dense and sparse kernel variants. The focus was conversational, prefix-heavy workloads with bursty tail (multi-message turns) to stress KV cache behavior and kernel scheduling under capacity pressure.

Motivation:
- Prior benches focused on absolute throughput. Product needs a simple decision tree to pick quant + kernel profiles for customers with hard latency SLOs (p95/p99) while minimizing unit cost.
- We want to capture the worst-case tail and quality regressions that matter for chat agents (precision in instruction-following and hallucination rate).
- Sparse kernels have shown promising speedups on long-context, but we haven't measured SLA impact under bursty arrival and mixed model variants.

Testbed and Constraints:
- Hardware: g5.12x (A100 equivalent emulation), driver stack pinned to runtime-2024.3. Kernel scheduler config: default dispatch with tuned occupancy w/ 80% GPU steer.
- Serving runtime: local branch runtime/quant-sla-experiment (see PR link).
- Models: small/medium LLMs used to keep experiment repeatable — Llama-2-13B (baseline float32), Redwood-curated-13B-v1 (open checkpoint used for quant), and a distilled 7B conversational variant for long-turn stress tests.
- Quant methods evaluated: INT8-linear (per-channel), GPTQ (8-bit greedy cluster — baseline for quality), AWQ-block (8-bit asymmetric, block size 128), FP8-e4m3-equivalent (simulated), plus two hybrid profiles (INT8 for attention + FP8 for MLP; AWQ fallback mix).
- Kernels: dense GEMM kernels (baseline), blocked sparse GEMMs (2:1 structured sparsity emulation), vector-lane optimized kernels (our internal fast-path), and a fallback interpreter.
- Workloads: 1) Spike-chat: 30s bursts of 400 concurrent short-chat requests, 2) Long-turn assistant: 16-turn conversations with heavy prefix context (avg 2.5k tokens), 3) Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mock with repeated prefix and high cache hit ratio.
- Metrics: latency p50/p95/p99, CPU and GPU utilization, tokens/sec (effective), cost-per-token estimate (runtime-cost model), quality: perplexity on held-out instruction set + short automated correctness suite (binary pass/fail on 100 golden QAs), and an LLM-judge pairwise score on 200 samples to approximate hallucination/faithfulness.

Methodology:
- Each profile run for 30 min steady-state after warmup; each experiment repeated 3x and we collect aggregated quantiles.
- KV cache warm/warmless experiments: cold-start (no KV cached), warm (cache populated from previous requests), and cache-thrash (alternating keys to force eviction).
- For quality: decoded 8 greedy + sampled decoding for judge runs; same seeds across quant variants.
- Scheduler conditions: unconstrained (ample quota), constrained (deliberate cap to force kernel contention), and emergency-fallback scenario (simulate a model variant outage to check graceful fallback).

High-level results (synth):
- INT8-linear dense: lowest degradation in quality vs baseline (avg perplexity +2.3%). Latency: moderate improvements vs FP32 (p95 ~15% down), cost savings ~32%. Under constrained scheduler with cache-thrash, p99 spikes increase by 40% vs unconstrained.
- AWQ-block (block-size=128): best raw token throughput in long-turn warm-cache scenarios (up to 1.6x tokens/sec vs INT8 dense) when using vector-lane kernels. However AWQ showed a measurable quality hit on the QA correctness suite (failures increased from 6% -> 14%). p99 under burst was volatile — sparse kernel jittered more under mixed work.
- FP8-sim: largest latency wins for short-turn conversational low-context requests (p50 reduced by ~22%), but quality regressions were model sensitive — medium for instruction-following. Cost savings similar to INT8 but slightly less stable across seeds.
- GPTQ baseline: quality closest to FP32 (fail rate 4%) but cost/latency improvements were smaller than AWQ/FP8.
- Hybrid (attn INT8 + mlp FP8): promising balance — retained much of GPTQ quality (fail 5–7%) while improving p95 by ~12% and cost by ~28%.
- Sparse kernels: huge wins on long-context warm-cache workloads when structured sparsity aligns with kernel-friendly layout (up to 2.2x throughput). But when arrival patterns broke kernel occupancy assumptions (bursty short requests interleaved), p99 tail worsened and jitter increased compared to dense kernels.

Notable observations and anecdotes:
- Cache-win amplification: AWQ + sparse kernels produce largest gains only when KV cache hit-rate > 70%. In cache-thrash cycles, the cost advantage collapses and p99 degrades more than INT8 dense.
- Kernel hop penalty: switching between vector-lane optimized kernels and fallback interpreter inside a batch can add 3–9ms median penalty that compounds at high concurrency (observed as p95 jumps).
- Deterministic failure modes: AWQ block quant at block alignment boundaries produced occasional token-level hallucination patterns (short path repetition) on ~0.4% of eval samples — reproducible with same seed.
- Scheduler fairness: under constrained quota, sparse kernels monopolized a GPU when a large long-turn request arrived, starving short-chat and causing SLO violations. We observed a need for route-aware queuing or preemption.

Actionable takeaways (recommendations):
1) For strict p99 SLOs (e.g., p99 < 300ms): default to INT8-linear dense profiles with vector-lane kernels; reserve AWQ/sparse profiles for customers with long-context, high cache-hit usage patterns and looser tail SLOs.
2) Offer a hybrid preset (attn INT8 + mlp FP8) as a standard profile for customers that want a middle ground with predictable tails.
3) Add kernel-occupancy telemetry (per-request kernel path ID + timestamp) into token traces so we can auto-detect kernel-hopping penalties in prod.
4) Implement preemptive scheduling policy: short-tail-first for p99-bound routes when mixed with long-turn jobs. Add config knob to pin long-turn workloads to dedicated pools.
5) AWQ validation: add unit tests for block-alignment edge cases and seed-based hallucination regression checks to our eval harness.
6) Cost estimator: expose per-route modeled cost under cold vs warm KV cache assumptions; highlight when sparse kernels trigger higher risk of p99 regressions.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How different are these observations on other GPU types (H100 vs A100)? Need cross-arch run.
- Can we automate a profile matcher that selects dense vs sparse kernels based on observed cache-hit ratio and request-size histogram?
- What is the minimal block size for AWQ that avoids hallucination artifacts while still yielding speedups?

Appendix: raw numbers (excerpt)
- Runtime-cost model assumptions: $X per GPU-hour normalized to token-step cost using measured tokens/sec.
- Example per-profile aggregated numbers (long-turn warm-cache):
  * INT8-dense: p50=120ms, p95=230ms, p99=310ms, cost/token=0.00092, QA-fail=6%
  * AWQ-sparse: p50=95ms, p95=185ms, p99=520ms, cost/token=0.00063, QA-fail=14%
  * FP8-dense: p50=92ms, p95=210ms, p99=340ms, cost/token=0.00097, QA-fail=9%
  * Hybrid (INT8-attn+FP8-mlp): p50=110ms, p95=200ms, p99=330ms, cost/token=0.00084, QA-fail=7%

Lab notes / run ids:
- Runs: sla-sweep-20240514-{01..09}, warm/cold toggles; seed 42 for judge runs.
- Profiling tools: custom microprofiler + Nsight flame snapshots, internal kernel-tracer v0.9.

Immediate next steps:
- PR to add kernel path telemetry (github link in linked artifacts).
- Short follow-up sweep on H100-sim host to validate cross-arch behavior.
- Draft a short internal one-pager for Solutions Eng recommending default profile per customer SLA.

Notes-to-self (rough):
- Re-run AWQ block-size 64 vs 128; instrument for token-repetition artifacts.
- Add preemption experiments with a 2-level queue (short vs long) and measure p99 improvement.
- Discuss long-turn dedicated pools with infra (cost tradeoffs).

References / links: see linked_artifacts above and PR notes in github.
